detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.name: MISO
sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.name: Southwest Power Pool
sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The five regional queues captured here — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, SPP, and CAISO — cover different slices of the US grid and cannot be added together to produce a national total, since each operator defines its scope differently and tracks projects at different stages from early study through commissioning. That said, the sheer volume of capacity waiting to connect is striking within each region on its own terms. ERCOT's Texas queue alone holds 438,087 MW across 1,778 requests, with storage at 159,820 MW and gas at 78,092 MW leading behind solar's 150,347 MW. MISO shows 299,721 MW across 3,828 requests, SPP 198,716 MW across 1,075 requests, NYISO 319,095 MW across 1,414 requests, and CAISO 71,682 MW across 265 active requests. These are planned generation and storage projects seeking grid access, not measurements of data center demand, but the composition of each queue offers indirect signals about where load growth is expected.

Storage and gas additions are the fuel types most directly tied to serving large, around-the-clock loads like AI data centers, because solar and wind alone cannot guarantee the firm power those facilities require. In ERCOT, storage requests total 159,820 MW and gas 78,092 MW, the largest absolute figures across any single queue in this snapshot. SPP carries 52,913 MW of storage and 47,392 MW of gas despite having far fewer total requests than MISO, suggesting concentrated bets on dispatchable power in that footprint. CAISO's queue is smaller in total megawatts but heavily weighted toward storage at 46,944 MW, reflecting California's policy environment. MISO shows 68,429 MW of storage and 30,236 MW of gas queued across its broad Midcontinent territory. These patterns suggest developers are positioning firm and flexible capacity in Texas, the south-central US, and the Midwest, regions where several states with significant commercial electricity sales also appear in the EIA data.

On the demand side, EIA commercial-sector electricity sales for June 2026 — a proxy for, not a direct measure of, data center consumption — show Texas reporting the highest figure among the eight states listed at 15,754 gigawatt-hours, followed by California at 10,025 GWh, Ohio at 5,588 GWh, Georgia at 5,547 GWh, and Virginia at 7,771 GWh; prices ranged from a low of $8.66 per megawatt-hour in Texas to $27.33 in California, a spread that helps explain why so much interconnection activity is concentrated in lower-cost regions. Virginia's 7,771 GWh at $10.99 reflects its dense data center corridor even though no dedicated Virginia-focused queue operator appears in this snapshot. The geographic overlap between states with high commercial sales and states within high-storage, high-gas queue footprints is the clearest signal in this data set of where grid planners and developers expect AI-driven load to land.

The single most important thing to watch in coming months is whether gas interconnection requests in ERCOT and SPP advance from study into active construction agreements, since that movement would confirm that developers are committing capital — not just filing paperwork — to serve the firm power needs that large AI data centers require.
